stem: How is the fuel ignited in a running diesel engine?
option_a: By glow plugs that stay switched on while the engine runs
option_b: By the injector heating the fuel as it sprays it
option_c: By the heat of the compressed air in the cylinder
option_d: By a spark plug in each cylinder
explanation: Diesels rely on compression ignition. Squeezing the air makes it hot enough to ignite the fuel as soon as it is injected.

stem: What does moving the throttle lever on a diesel engine actually change?
option_a: How far a butterfly valve in the air intake is opened
option_b: The speed of the camshaft compared with the crankshaft
option_c: The timing of the spark
option_d: The amount of fuel injected into each cylinder
explanation: A diesel's speed and power are set by the quantity of fuel injected. Unlike a petrol engine, it does not throttle the incoming air.

stem: Why does a diesel engine need a high compression ratio?
option_a: To keep the cylinders cool while the engine is running
option_b: To heat the air enough to ignite the fuel
option_c: To raise the engine's oil pressure
option_d: To push more fuel through the injectors
explanation: The air must be squeezed hard to reach a temperature well above the point at which diesel fuel ignites on its own.

stem: An engine's compression ratio is given as 18 to 1. What does that figure describe?
option_a: Fuel is injected at 18 times the pressure of the outside air
option_b: The space above the piston shrinks to an eighteenth as it rises
option_c: There are 18 parts of air to every part of fuel burnt in the cylinder
option_d: The crankshaft turns 18 times for every power stroke in each cylinder
explanation: The compression ratio compares the space above the piston at the bottom of its stroke with the space left at the top. Many conventional small diesels are somewhere around 15:1 to 23:1, but that is a typical range, not a specification.

stem: What is the correct order of the four strokes?
option_a: Induction, power, compression, exhaust
option_b: Induction, compression, power, exhaust
option_c: Compression, induction, exhaust, then power
option_d: Power, induction, exhaust, compression
explanation: Air is drawn in, compressed, burnt with the fuel to drive the piston down, and then pushed out as exhaust.

stem: How many times does the crankshaft turn during one complete four-stroke cycle?
option_a: Four times
option_b: Once
option_c: Twice
option_d: Half a turn
explanation: Each stroke is half a turn of the crankshaft, so four strokes take two full revolutions.

stem: When is fuel injected into the cylinder?
option_a: At the very start of the induction stroke
option_b: Near the end of the compression stroke
option_c: During the exhaust stroke
option_d: At the bottom of the power stroke
explanation: Fuel is sprayed in just before the piston reaches the top of the compression stroke, when the air is at its hottest.

stem: What does a diesel engine draw into the cylinder on the induction stroke?
option_a: A mixture of air and fuel
option_b: Air mixed with a fine mist of lubricating oil
option_c: Air only
option_d: Fuel only
explanation: Only air is drawn in. The fuel is added later by the injector, directly into the hot compressed air.

stem: How fast does the camshaft turn compared with the crankshaft?
option_a: At half the crankshaft speed
option_b: At the same speed
option_c: At a quarter of the crankshaft speed
option_d: At twice the crankshaft speed
explanation: Each valve opens once per cycle, and a cycle takes two crankshaft turns, so the camshaft turns once for every two turns of the crank.

stem: Which part turns the up-and-down movement of the pistons into rotation?
option_a: The flywheel
option_b: The injection pump
option_c: The crankshaft
option_d: The camshaft
explanation: Connecting rods link each piston to the crankshaft, which converts their reciprocating motion into rotation.

stem: What is the job of the fuel injection pump?
option_a: To lift fuel from the tank up to the primary filter
option_b: To send unused fuel from the injectors back to the tank
option_c: To deliver fuel at high pressure to each injector at the right time
option_d: To separate any water from the fuel before the filters
explanation: The injection pump meters, pressurises and times the fuel for each cylinder. Lifting fuel from the tank is the lift pump's job.

stem: Where are the inlet and exhaust valves usually found?
option_a: In the cylinder head
option_b: In the fuel injection pump
option_c: In the sump
option_d: In the cylinder block, beside the crankshaft
explanation: The cylinder head sits on top of the block and carries the valves and the injectors.

stem: Which of these is a job of the flywheel?
option_a: Driving the raw water pump through a toothed belt
option_b: Pumping oil round the engine
option_c: Setting the timing of each injection
option_d: Smoothing out the pulses from each power stroke
explanation: The flywheel's weight carries the engine through the non-power strokes. Its toothed ring also gives the starter motor something to turn.

stem: What seals the joint between the cylinder head and the cylinder block?
option_a: The sump gasket
option_b: The rocker cover seal
option_c: The exhaust manifold gasket
option_d: The head gasket
explanation: The head gasket keeps compression, oil and coolant in their proper places where the head meets the block.

stem: What should you do before reaching into the engine space to find its parts?
option_a: Run the engine so you can hear where each part is
option_b: Remove the drive belts
option_c: Close the fuel tank valve and then bleed the fuel system
option_d: Make sure the engine is stopped and cannot be started
explanation: Stop the engine and remove the key or isolate it, so nobody can start it while your hands are near belts and pulleys. Reaching into a running engine is dangerous: belts and pulleys can trap fingers and clothing in an instant.

stem: Why is it worth knowing exactly where the raw water seacock is before you need it?
option_a: Because the gearbox oil level is checked beside it
option_b: So you can open it to top up the engine's coolant
option_c: So you can close it to stop the engine quickly in an emergency
option_d: So you can close it fast if a hose fails, or before working on the circuit
explanation: The seacock lets sea water into the engine's cooling circuit. Being able to shut it fast can stop a leak becoming a flood. Closing it is not a way to stop the engine: running with it closed quickly damages the pump and the exhaust.

stem: Where would you normally check the engine oil level?
option_a: At the raw water strainer
option_b: On the engine oil dipstick
option_c: On the primary fuel filter bowl
option_d: In the coolant header tank
explanation: The dipstick shows the oil level in the sump. Check it with the engine stopped and the boat as level as possible.

stem: Why can a worn engine with poor compression be hard to start from cold?
option_a: The starter motor is designed to cut out whenever compression is low
option_b: The air is not squeezed enough to get hot enough to ignite the fuel
option_c: The injectors cannot open without full compression
option_d: Low compression lets too much oil reach the fuel
explanation: A diesel relies on the heat of compression to light its fuel. If air leaks past worn rings or valves, it does not get hot enough, and a cold engine makes this worse because the metal soaks up heat.

stem: When you trace the fuel line on many installations, what will you often find between the tank and the engine-mounted filter?
option_a: The engine oil filter
option_b: A primary filter, often with a water trap
option_c: The heat exchanger and header tank
option_d: The raw water strainer and its removable basket
explanation: Many installations have a primary filter with a water trap before the finer filter on the engine, although layouts vary and not every boat has one in the same place. The strainer, heat exchanger and oil filter belong to the cooling and lubrication systems.

stem: Why is it useful to keep labelled photos or a sketch of your engine on board?
option_a: So you can find parts quickly when something goes wrong
option_b: So a surveyor can value the engine
option_c: So the engine warranty stays valid
option_d: Because it is a legal requirement for all boats with engines
explanation: Faults tend to happen at awkward moments. A labelled picture saves time finding the dipstick, filters or seacock when you are under pressure. It is a good habit, not a legal or warranty requirement.

stem: Why does the fuel pick-up pipe usually stop a little above the bottom of the tank?
option_a: So the fuel stays warmer on its way to the engine in cold weather
option_b: So the tank vent cannot be blocked by fuel when the tank is full
option_c: So that a reserve of fuel is kept back for emergencies
option_d: So water and sludge that settle at the bottom are less likely to be drawn in
explanation: Water is heavier than diesel and dirt settles out, so both collect at the bottom of the tank. Drawing from slightly higher up keeps most of it out of the fuel system.

stem: Why does a small leak on the suction side of the fuel system often cause the engine to stop rather than drip fuel?
option_a: Because the injection pump senses the leak and shuts the engine down to protect it
option_b: Because the suction draws air in through the leak instead of pushing fuel out
option_c: Because the return line keeps refilling the leak with fresh fuel
option_d: Because diesel evaporates from the joint before it has time to drip
explanation: Between the tank and the lift pump the fuel is under suction, so a loose joint pulls air in. That air reaches the injection pump, which cannot build pressure with air in it.

stem: What is the purpose of the fuel return or leak-off line?
option_a: To drain water from the bottom of the tank down into the primary filter bowl
option_b: To carry spare fuel, and any air it has picked up, back to the tank
option_c: To let air into the tank as the fuel level goes down
option_d: To carry fuel from the deck filler down into the tank
explanation: The injection system is given more fuel than it burns. The surplus, along with any air bubbles, flows back to the tank. Letting air into the tank is the vent's job.

stem: Why can even a small bubble of air stop a diesel engine?
option_a: Air reacts with diesel in the lines and turns it into a thick wax
option_b: Air makes the fuel ignite too early, inside the lift pump itself
option_c: Air gets trapped in the filter element and blocks it completely
option_d: Air compresses, so the pump cannot build enough pressure to open the injectors
explanation: Liquid fuel barely compresses, which is how the pump builds very high pressure. Air squashes like a spring instead, so the pressure needed to open the injector is not reached.

stem: Where does water collect in a primary fuel filter with a clear bowl?
option_a: At the top of the bowl, floating above the fuel
option_b: At the bottom of the bowl, below the fuel
option_c: Mixed evenly through the fuel
option_d: Soaked into the paper filter element
explanation: Water is denser than diesel, so it sinks and forms a separate layer at the bottom of the bowl, where it can be seen and drained off.

stem: You see a layer of water in the primary filter bowl. What should you do?
option_a: With the engine stopped, drain it into a container until clean fuel runs out
option_b: Drain it into the bilge so the bilge pump can take it away
option_c: Run the engine hard for an hour so that the water is burnt off
option_d: Leave it there, because the engine's fine filter will catch it further along
explanation: Water must be removed before it reaches the injection equipment. Drain it into a container, never into the bilge, because fuel-contaminated water must not be pumped overboard. Running the engine to 'burn off' water is not safe: water reaching the injection pump can damage it or stop the engine at sea.

stem: Why does a diesel engine have two stages of fuel filter?
option_a: Two filters let the engine run on two different grades of fuel without any changes
option_b: The first catches water and larger dirt, so the finer second one can take out tiny particles
option_c: The second filter is a spare that only starts working if the first one becomes blocked
option_d: One filter cleans the fuel going to the engine and the other cleans fuel returning to the tank
explanation: Removing the water and bigger particles first protects the fine filter, which then takes out the very small particles that would damage the injection pump and injectors.

stem: After changing a fuel filter element, what will the engine usually need before it runs properly?
option_a: The fuel system bled to remove the air let in
option_b: A new set of injectors fitted and pressure tested
option_c: The engine oil and oil filter changed
option_d: The raw water strainer cleaned out
explanation: Opening a filter lets air into the fuel system. Unless the engine is self-bleeding, that air must be pushed out before the injection pump can work.

stem: What is the main job of the lift pump?
option_a: To pump any water out of the bottom of the fuel tank
option_b: To spray a fine mist of fuel into each of the cylinders
option_c: To draw fuel from the tank and feed it to the injection pump
option_d: To raise the fuel to the very high pressure needed for injection
explanation: The lift pump works on the low-pressure side, keeping the injection pump supplied. Creating the very high injection pressure is the injection pump's job.

stem: How are many mechanically injected small marine diesels stopped?
option_a: By cutting off the fuel at the injection pump
option_b: By switching off the battery isolator
option_c: By switching off the glow plugs
option_d: By closing the fuel valve at the tank
explanation: The stop control, a cable or solenoid, shuts off fuel delivery at the injection pump. Closing the tank valve would take a long time and lets air in, glow plugs only help starting, and switching off the isolator with the engine running can damage the alternator. Electronically controlled engines are stopped through their control system.

stem: Why should you never feel for a leak along a high-pressure fuel pipe with your hand?
option_a: The fuel is under enough pressure to pierce skin and cause serious injury
option_b: The pipe can crack if it is touched while the engine is running
option_c: The pipes carry an electrical current while the engine is running, as part of the stop circuit
option_d: Oils from your skin make the steel fuel pipes corrode quickly
explanation: A fine jet of fuel from a high-pressure leak can be injected through the skin. This is a medical emergency, so look for leaks visually or with a piece of card instead.

stem: Which of these is a typical sign of a faulty injector?
option_a: Black smoke and rough running, sometimes with a knock from one cylinder
option_b: Blue smoke that gets worse after long periods at idle
option_c: Black smoke only at full load that clears once the air filter is changed
option_d: Steam and very little water coming out of the exhaust
explanation: An injector that dribbles or sprays poorly delivers fuel that does not burn completely, giving smoke, rough running and sometimes a knock. Black smoke cured by a new air filter points to the air supply, blue smoke to oil, and steam to cooling.

stem: With the engine running, you see a fine mist of fuel around one of the injector pipes. What should you do?
option_a: Open it, because owners can safely bleed at any connection on a fuel system
option_b: Stop and check the handbook; leave the high-pressure side to an engineer
option_c: Feel along the pipe while the engine turns to see whether it is under pressure
option_d: Loosen it slightly while someone cranks, to see whether fuel spurts out
explanation: Fuel from a high-pressure leak can be injected through the skin, and the spray is a fire risk. Stop the engine, keep clear, contain any spill and do not restart until a qualified engineer has repaired it. Suspected injection injury needs emergency medical treatment.

stem: Which of these usually means the fuel system will need bleeding?
option_a: The engine ran out of fuel
option_b: The engine oil was changed
option_c: The raw water impeller was replaced
option_d: The alternator belt was adjusted
explanation: Running the tank dry lets air into the fuel lines. Oil changes, belt work and impeller changes do not open the fuel system.

stem: In what order should you work through the bleed points?
option_a: In any order you like, as long as every bleed point gets opened
option_b: All the points opened at once, then closed together at the end
option_c: From the point nearest the tank towards the engine, following the fuel's path
option_d: From the injectors back towards the tank, against the fuel's flow
explanation: Fuel pushes air ahead of it along the system. Starting near the tank clears each section in turn; starting at the far end just draws more air through from behind.

stem: When should you close a bleed screw?
option_a: After the pump has stopped and fuel has stopped flowing
option_b: As soon as the first drop of fuel appears
option_c: While fuel free of bubbles is still flowing out
option_d: Only once the engine has started
explanation: Closing while clean fuel is still flowing stops air being drawn back in. The first drops often still carry bubbles, so keep pumping until they stop.

stem: The hand lever on a cam-operated mechanical lift pump has almost no movement. What is a likely reason?
option_a: The fuel valve at the tank has been left closed
option_b: The lift pump's diaphragm has split
option_c: The engine's cam is holding the pump's arm at the top of its travel
option_d: The primary filter is blocked, so the pump cannot draw fuel
explanation: A mechanical lift pump is worked by a cam on the engine. If the engine stopped with the cam lobe holding the arm, the hand lever has little travel; turning the engine a little frees it. A closed valve, blocked filter or split diaphragm stops fuel flowing but does not usually stop the lever moving. Electric lift pumps have no lever.

stem: You bleed the system, the engine runs for a few minutes, then stops again with the same symptoms. What should you suspect?
option_a: The engine needs a higher grade of oil before it will keep running for long
option_b: The bleeding was done while the engine was too cold
option_c: Air is still getting in somewhere, so the cause has not been found
option_d: The injection pump was damaged when the tank ran dry
explanation: Bleeding removes air but does not stop it entering. If air returns, look for a loose joint, a damaged seal, a split hose on the suction side or a low tank.

stem: While bleeding, you are not sure whether the next connection is on the low-pressure or the high-pressure side. What should you do?
option_a: Stop and check the handbook, and leave anything on the high-pressure side to a qualified engineer
option_b: Open it, because owners can safely bleed at any connection on a fuel system
option_c: Loosen it slightly while someone cranks, to see whether fuel spurts out
option_d: Feel along the pipe while the engine turns to see whether it is under pressure
explanation: Owner bleeding is limited to the handbook's low-pressure points. High-pressure fuel can penetrate skin and cause severe injury, so if you are unsure, stop and check, and use a qualified engineer for anything else.

stem: What is diesel bug?
option_a: A fault in the injection pump's electronic control unit
option_b: An insect that gets into fuel tanks through the breather vent
option_c: Micro-organisms that grow where water meets fuel in the tank, forming sludge
option_d: A wax that forms in diesel fuel, but only during very cold weather in winter
explanation: Bacteria and fungi live at the boundary between water and fuel. They feed on the fuel and form a slime that blocks filters. Cold-weather waxing is a separate problem.

stem: Why do engines with fuel contamination often stop in rough weather?
option_a: The injection pump cannot work properly when the boat heels over
option_b: Cold spray thickens the fuel in the lines until it can no longer flow
option_c: Waves force diesel out of the tank through the vent, so it runs low
option_d: The motion stirs up water and sludge from the tank bottom, which blocks the filters
explanation: In calm conditions, dirt and water sit undisturbed below the pick-up. Rough water churns them into the fuel, and the filters block soon afterwards.

stem: Which of these helps most to stop water getting into the fuel tank?
option_a: Draining the primary filter bowl more often
option_b: Keeping the deck filler cap seal in good condition
option_c: Adding a biocide every time you refuel
option_d: Fitting a second fine filter on the engine
explanation: A worn filler seal lets rain and spray straight into the tank. A biocide treats the effects of water, draining the bowl removes water that has already got in, and an extra filter does nothing to keep it out.

stem: A tank is badly contaminated with diesel bug. Why are additives alone not enough?
option_a: Additives only start to work once the engine runs at full power for hours
option_b: Additives make the fuel too thick for the lift pump to draw it
option_c: They may kill the organisms, but the existing sludge stays and keeps blocking filters
option_d: Additives are designed for petrol engines and have no effect in diesel
explanation: A biocide can stop further growth, but the dead sludge remains and will still block filters. A badly affected tank needs the fuel polished or the tank cleaned.

stem: In an indirectly cooled engine, what circulates through the engine block?
option_a: Air blown by a fan
option_b: Engine oil only
option_c: Sea water drawn through the hull inlet
option_d: Coolant in a closed circuit
explanation: Indirect cooling keeps a closed circuit of coolant in the engine. The sea water passes through the heat exchanger and the exhaust, so in normal operation salt does not reach the block.

stem: What is the main advantage of indirect cooling over direct cooling?
option_a: It removes the need for a seacock on the cooling inlet
option_b: It lets the engine run without a thermostat
option_c: Salt water is kept out of the engine, reducing corrosion and scale
option_d: It does away with the raw water pump and its impeller
explanation: Sea water is corrosive and leaves deposits. With indirect cooling, only the raw water side (pump, heat exchanger and exhaust) sees sea water, which protects the engine's internal passages. A raw water pump and seacock are still needed.

stem: On a typical wet-exhaust installation, what happens to the raw water after it has cooled the engine?
option_a: It is mixed with the engine coolant in the header tank
option_b: It returns to the sea through the same seacock it came in by
option_c: It is sprayed into the exhaust and leaves the boat with the gases
option_d: It drains into the bilge, where the automatic bilge pump removes it
explanation: Spraying the water into the exhaust cools the hot gas so the exhaust can run through rubber hose and a water-lock silencer, and it is why you see water coming out with the exhaust.

stem: Why are directly cooled engines usually designed to run cooler than indirectly cooled ones?
option_a: To make the engine use less fuel
option_b: Because the raw water pump cannot move hot water fast enough
option_c: To limit salt coming out of the sea water and building up inside the engine
option_d: Because sea water boils at a lower temperature than fresh water
explanation: Salt and minerals come out of sea water faster as it gets hotter, forming scale that blocks passages. Running cooler slows this, though a cooler engine is less efficient.

stem: What must you do before opening the raw water strainer?
option_a: Open the coolant pressure cap
option_b: Stop the engine and close the seacock
option_c: Run the engine for a while to warm up the water
option_d: Disconnect the battery
explanation: With the seacock open, water can pour in through the strainer, because it is below the waterline on many boats. Stopping the engine also stops the pump running dry. Opening the strainer with the seacock open can flood the boat, and opening a hot coolant pressure cap can spray scalding coolant.

stem: The strainer lid seal is leaking air. What can this cause?
option_a: Diesel leaks into the cooling water through the strainer lid
option_b: The impeller runs faster and wears out sooner
option_c: The raw water pump loses suction and the engine overheats
option_d: The engine oil becomes diluted with sea water
explanation: The pump draws water through the strainer. If the lid lets air in, the pump draws air instead of water, so the flow drops or stops and the engine overheats.

stem: Why should you work the seacock handle from time to time?
option_a: To flush salt deposits out of the engine's internal water passages
option_b: To push fresh coolant round into the header tank
option_c: To keep the raw water pump's impeller lubricated
option_d: So it does not seize and can be closed quickly in an emergency
explanation: Seacocks left in one position can seize with growth and corrosion. If a hose fails, you need to be able to close it at once.

stem: What is the purpose of an anti-siphon valve in the raw water circuit?
option_a: To stop diesel siphoning out of the fuel tank
option_b: To let trapped air out of the coolant circuit
option_c: To increase the flow of cooling water to the heat exchanger
option_d: To stop sea water siphoning back into a stopped engine
explanation: Where the engine is near or below the waterline, water can siphon through the circuit and fill the exhaust and cylinders. The valve lets air into the top of the loop to break the siphon.

stem: Which is the right approach to securing a hose on a below-waterline fitting?
option_a: Fit as many clips as will go on the spigot
option_b: Use any clip, as long as it is tightened as hard as possible
option_c: Fit two stainless clips at each end, whatever the hose or fitting
option_d: Use the clamp type, size, number and placement the maker specifies
explanation: Hoses on hull openings must suit the installation, be correctly secured and be inspected regularly. Double clamping is not a universal substitute for correct fit and installation, and overtightening can damage the hose.

stem: What is a raw water pump impeller usually made of?
option_a: Ceramic
option_b: Hardened stainless steel
option_c: Cast iron
option_d: Flexible rubber
explanation: The vanes need to bend and straighten as the impeller turns off-centre in the pump body, which is why it is made of flexible rubber, and why it wears out.

stem: What damages an impeller most quickly?
option_a: Using the engine in fresh water
option_b: Running the engine in very cold water
option_c: Running the engine at low revs
option_d: Running the pump without water
explanation: The water lubricates and cools the rubber vanes. Without it they overheat and tear within moments, for example if the seacock is left closed.

stem: Your old impeller has two vanes missing. What should you do before running the engine?
option_a: Find the missing pieces, which have probably lodged further along
option_b: Fit the new impeller and check the flow, because small pieces pass through harmlessly
option_c: Nothing, because the rubber pieces will soon dissolve in the water
option_d: Run the engine hard for a while to flush the pieces out
explanation: Broken vanes travel downstream and often block the heat exchanger inlet, causing overheating even with a new impeller. They do not break down on their own, and running the engine hard to flush them out drives them further in and can overheat the engine.

stem: Why can impellers fail early in the season after a long lay-up?
option_a: The vanes take a set while standing and can crack when they start working again
option_b: The impeller shrinks over winter and comes loose on its shaft
option_c: The pump's drive belt slips for the first few hours of the season
option_d: The pump's shaft seal dries out, so the impeller slips on its shaft
explanation: Vanes held bent in one position for months set in that shape and lose their flexibility, so they crack or tear soon after recommissioning. Some owners fit a new impeller in spring, or remove it for the winter where the handbook allows; practice varies between engines.

stem: When should you check the coolant level in the header tank?
option_a: With the engine running, once the temperature gauge reads normal
option_b: When the engine is cold
option_c: While the engine is running at full power
option_d: Immediately after stopping a hot engine
explanation: A hot coolant circuit is under pressure, and removing the cap can release scalding coolant. Checking cold is safe and gives a consistent reading.

stem: On a typical indirectly cooled engine, what does the thermostat do when the engine is cold?
option_a: Turns on the glow plugs until the coolant reaches working temperature
option_b: Opens fully so that the heat exchanger can start cooling the engine straight away
option_c: Lets raw water into the engine block so that it warms up more evenly
option_d: Stays closed so coolant only circulates round the engine, warming it quickly
explanation: By keeping coolant away from the heat exchanger at first, the thermostat helps the engine reach its working temperature sooner. It opens as the engine warms.

stem: Why is the coolant circuit kept under pressure by the cap?
option_a: To raise the boiling point of the coolant
option_b: To stop the thermostat opening
option_c: To push coolant into the exhaust
option_d: To keep air out of the raw water circuit
explanation: The higher the pressure, the higher the temperature a liquid can reach before it boils. This lets the engine run at its proper temperature without the coolant boiling.

stem: The engine runs at a normal temperature at low revs but overheats under load, and the raw water flow looks normal. Which is a likely cause?
option_a: A raw water seacock that has been left closed
option_b: A blocked fuel filter starving the engine
option_c: An impeller that is missing all of its vanes
option_d: A scaled heat exchanger or a sticking thermostat
explanation: A closed seacock or missing impeller would stop the water flow altogether. When flow is normal but the engine overheats only when working hard, heat is not being transferred well enough.

stem: Straight after starting, what tells you the raw water circuit is working?
option_a: Cooling water coming out with the exhaust
option_b: The oil pressure warning light going out
option_c: The temperature gauge reading normal straight away
option_d: The charge warning light going out
explanation: Water from the exhaust shows the raw water circuit is working. If there is none, stop the engine before the impeller and exhaust are damaged. The warning lights tell you about oil pressure and charging, and the gauge takes several minutes to rise.

stem: Why is it worth learning where your temperature gauge normally sits?
option_a: So you notice a slow rise early, before it becomes serious
option_b: Because the needle should sit exactly halfway on every engine
option_c: So you can set the throttle by its reading instead
option_d: Because the reading tells you when the oil needs changing
explanation: Every engine settles at its own normal reading. A slow drift above it is often the first sign of a blocked strainer, worn impeller or scaled heat exchanger.

stem: You hear a belt squealing and the temperature starts to rise. What is the link?
option_a: The belt may also drive the coolant pump, so slipping cuts coolant flow
option_b: There is no link, so the temperature rise is a coincidence
option_c: The noise is caused by steam building up in the exhaust
option_d: The alternator is overcharging and heating the engine
explanation: On many engines one belt drives both the alternator and the coolant circulating pump. If it slips, the pump slows and the engine gets hotter.

stem: There is steam and very little water from the exhaust. Why is stopping the engine also important for the exhaust system itself?
option_a: Steam travels back up the exhaust and condenses in the fuel filter, blocking it
option_b: Without water, hot exhaust gas can melt the rubber hoses and silencer
option_c: The steam makes the propeller lose its grip on the water
option_d: Steam cools the exhaust too much and cracks the manifold
explanation: Wet exhaust systems use rubber hose and plastic or composite silencers that rely on the injected water to stay cool. Hot, dry exhaust gas can melt or burn them, risking fire and fumes inside the boat.

stem: The overheat alarm sounds as you motor out of a busy harbour. Which order of actions is best?
option_a: Keep motoring to a quiet berth, then stop and investigate once tied up
option_b: Get the boat safe, stop the engine, let it cool, then check the cooling
option_c: Check the strainer with the engine running, and stop only if it is clear
option_d: Open the coolant pressure cap to check the level, then reduce power
explanation: Overheating is a stop-engine condition. Get the boat safe, reduce power and stop as soon as it is safe, and let the engine cool before you open anything. A hot pressure cap can spray scalding coolant, opening the strainer with the engine running can flood the boat or run the pump dry, and running on can cause serious damage.

stem: Where is the engine oil stored when it is not circulating?
option_a: In the header tank fitted on top of the engine
option_b: In the sump at the bottom of the engine
option_c: In a separate tank beside the fuel tank
option_d: Inside the heat exchanger tubes
explanation: Oil drains back to the sump after lubricating the engine, and the oil pump draws it from there. The header tank holds coolant, not oil.

stem: What does the oil filter remove?
option_a: Fine particles of soot and metal from the oil
option_b: Salt and weed from the raw cooling water
option_c: Air bubbles that have been trapped in the engine coolant
option_d: Water that has separated out of the fuel
explanation: The oil filter traps particles that would otherwise wear the bearings. Water in fuel is caught by the fuel filter, and the cooling system has its own strainer.

stem: Apart from reducing friction, which of these is a job of engine oil?
option_a: Keeping the fuel system free of air
option_b: Cooling the exhaust gases before they leave the boat's stern
option_c: Carrying heat away from hot parts such as the pistons
option_d: Cleaning the fuel injectors as it circulates
explanation: Oil also carries heat, holds dirt in suspension, helps the rings seal and protects against corrosion. Cooling the exhaust is done by the raw water.

stem: Why does diesel engine oil need changing even if the level stays correct?
option_a: Soot and acids build up in it and its additives get used up
option_b: The oil gets heavier and sinks below the pump's pick-up
option_c: The marks on the dipstick wear off and can no longer be read
option_d: Oil that has been heated many times turns into grease
explanation: A correct level says nothing about condition. Contamination and spent additives mean old oil protects the engine less well, so it is replaced at set intervals.

stem: What carries oil from the pump to the crankshaft and camshaft bearings?
option_a: The raw water hoses that run round the outside of the engine
option_b: Drilled passages in the engine called oil galleries
option_c: Channels cast into the exhaust manifold
option_d: The fuel return line from the injectors
explanation: Oil galleries are passages drilled through the block and head that deliver pressurised oil to the bearings and valve gear.

stem: When is the best time to check the engine oil level?
option_a: While the engine is running at idle in neutral
option_b: While motoring hard, when the oil is fully circulating
option_c: Before starting, with the engine cold and the boat level
option_d: Straight after stopping a hot engine, while the oil is thin
explanation: With the engine cold, all the oil has drained into the sump, and with the boat level the dipstick gives a true reading.

stem: Why do you wipe the dipstick and put it back before reading it?
option_a: To clean any dirt out of the inside of the dipstick tube
option_b: To warm the oil on the stick so that the level is easier to see
option_c: To let air into the sump so the oil settles evenly
option_d: Oil splashed on the stick gives a false reading the first time
explanation: The dipstick is often coated with oil above the real level. Wiping it and dipping again shows where the oil actually sits.

stem: The oil on the dipstick is black. What does this usually mean on a diesel?
option_a: The oil is burnt out and the engine is about to seize completely
option_b: The oil filter is missing or has not been fitted
option_c: Nothing unusual, because diesel oil darkens quickly with soot
option_d: Water has got into the oil from a leaking gasket
explanation: Diesel combustion produces soot, which the oil holds in suspension, so it turns dark soon after a change. Milky oil, not black oil, points to water.

stem: The oil on the dipstick looks milky and creamy. What does this suggest?
option_a: Fuel is diluting the oil
option_b: Water or coolant is getting into the oil
option_c: The oil has been overheated
option_d: The engine has been run at low revs for long periods
explanation: Water mixed with oil forms a creamy emulsion. It can come from coolant leaking internally or sea water getting in, and it needs investigating before the engine is run. Fuel dilution makes oil thin and smell of diesel rather than milky.

stem: You have not added any oil, but the level on the dipstick is higher than last week. What should you do?
option_a: Not run the engine until you find what is getting into the sump
option_b: Ignore it, because oil expands a little in warmer weather
option_c: Pump out the extra oil, then carry on using the engine
option_d: Run the engine hard for a while so that the extra oil burns off
explanation: A rising level shows that something else, usually fuel or water, is getting into the oil and diluting it. Running the engine with diluted oil risks serious damage.

stem: Where should you find the right oil grade and quantity for your engine?
option_a: From any oil marked as suitable for diesel engines
option_b: From the oil grade printed on the filter
option_c: In the engine manufacturer's handbook
option_d: From the colour of the old oil on the dipstick
explanation: Different engines need different oil specifications and quantities. The handbook is the reliable source; general-purpose oils may not meet the engine's needs.

stem: Why is the engine usually warmed up before the old oil is removed?
option_a: So the new filter's seal can seat properly
option_b: Cold oil cannot be pumped at all
option_c: Warm oil flows more easily and carries more dirt out with it
option_d: Warming the engine makes the oil filter release its trapped dirt
explanation: Warm oil is thinner, so more of it comes out and the soot and particles stay mixed in it rather than settling in the sump.

stem: When removing the old oil filter, what should you make sure of?
option_a: That the engine is running so the oil keeps flowing
option_b: That the old filter is still completely full of oil
option_c: That its old sealing ring has not stayed stuck to the engine
option_d: That the fuel valve is left open so the engine can restart easily
explanation: If the old seal stays on the engine and the new filter is fitted over it, the joint will not seal and oil can be pumped out quickly once the engine starts. Never change a filter with the engine running: hot oil sprays out under pressure and moving parts can catch you.

stem: Why does an engine that is used very little still need its oil changed regularly?
option_a: Standing oil grows the same organisms as diesel bug
option_b: Acids and moisture in old oil attack the engine while it stands
option_c: Oil evaporates from the sump within a few months
option_d: The oil filter swells and splits if it is not used
explanation: Combustion products in used oil form acids, and condensation adds water. Both cause corrosion inside an idle engine, which is why handbooks give a time limit as well as running hours.

stem: What should you do with the used oil and filter?
option_a: Pour the oil into the bilge to be pumped out
option_b: Put them in the general rubbish bin
option_c: Pour the oil over the side well away from land
option_d: Take them to a waste oil facility
explanation: Used oil is a pollutant. Marinas and recycling centres often have waste oil facilities; it must never go into the bilge, drains or water.

stem: The oil pressure warning comes on while you are motoring. What should you do?
option_a: Increase the revs to raise the pressure
option_b: Reduce power and stop the engine as soon as the boat is safe
option_c: Carry on and check the oil at the end of the trip
option_d: Stop, then restart after a minute to see whether the warning clears
explanation: Low oil pressure can wreck the bearings within minutes. Reduce power and stop as soon as the boat is safe, then check the oil level and look for leaks. Do not restart just to test whether the warning clears.

stem: The oil pressure lamp lights when you turn the key, before starting. What does this show?
option_a: The lamp and its circuit are working
option_b: The engine has no oil in the sump
option_c: The oil filter is blocked and needs changing
option_d: The battery is too flat to start
explanation: With the engine stopped there is no oil pressure, so the lamp should light. It should go out within a few seconds once the engine starts.

stem: The oil pressure warning came on and you have stopped the engine safely. What is a sensible first check?
option_a: Replace the oil pressure switch, which is probably faulty
option_b: Top up the oil to the maximum mark without checking the level
option_c: The oil level on the dipstick, and any obvious leaks
option_d: Restart the engine to see whether the warning clears
explanation: Once stopped, check the oil level and look for leaks as the handbook describes. Do not restart just to test the alarm, and do not assume the switch is at fault: a normal level does not prove the pressure is good.

stem: You suspect the oil pressure warning is caused by a faulty switch. What is the right approach?
option_a: Disconnect the switch and keep using the engine
option_b: Run the engine at higher revs, where the warning goes out
option_c: Treat the warning as real until the pressure has been checked properly
option_d: Assume the switch is faulty because the oil level is fine
explanation: A correct oil level does not prove the pressure is good. Only a test gauge shows the real pressure, so the warning should be trusted until then. Disconnecting the switch removes your only warning, and running on in the hope that it goes out risks the bearings.

stem: In a healthy engine, when does oil pressure tend to be at its lowest?
option_a: At full power once the engine is warm
option_b: At idle when the engine is fully warm
option_c: At high revs when the engine is still cold
option_d: Just after starting from cold
explanation: Hot oil is thinner and the pump turns slowly at idle, so pressure tends to be lowest then. This is why a borderline engine may show a warning only at hot idle. Actual readings and warning behaviour differ between engines and panels.

stem: The oil pressure alarm sounded and you stopped the engine. The dipstick shows the right level and there are no leaks. What should you do next?
option_a: Restart it, because a correct level shows the switch must be faulty
option_b: Leave the engine stopped and get the pressure checked, treating the warning as real
option_c: Restart and run at low revs to reach harbour, watching the light
option_d: Add oil above the maximum mark and restart
explanation: A normal level does not prove the pressure is good, and genuine low oil pressure risks the bearings. Do not restart simply to test whether the alarm clears; if the cause is not clear and corrected, get engineering assistance.

stem: Why do many boats keep a separate battery just for starting the engine?
option_a: So that using lights and equipment cannot leave you unable to start
option_b: So the engine can run without an alternator
option_c: Because the engine needs two batteries to turn over
option_d: Because domestic batteries cannot be charged by the engine's alternator
explanation: If the domestic bank is run flat overnight, the separate engine battery still has the charge needed to start, and the engine can then recharge both.

stem: The battery is fully charged but the starter only clicks. What should you check first?
option_a: That the raw water strainer basket is clear of weed
option_b: That the engine oil level is not too high
option_c: That nothing is caught round the propeller
option_d: That the battery terminals are clean and tight
explanation: A loose or corroded terminal cannot pass the heavy starting current, even from a good battery, so it behaves like a flat one.

stem: Why is a voltmeter reading of a battery's state of charge best taken after it has rested?
option_a: A battery gives no voltage reading at all while it is in use
option_b: The meter needs time to charge itself up from the battery first
option_c: Resting lets any gas escape so the meter can make contact
option_d: Recent charging or heavy use shifts the voltage, giving a misleading reading
explanation: Just after charging the voltage is higher than the true state of charge, and under load it is lower. After a rest it settles to a value that better reflects the charge.

stem: Why should sparks and flames be kept away from lead-acid batteries that are being charged?
option_a: A spark can reverse the battery's polarity
option_b: Heat from a flame makes the battery overcharge
option_c: Charging can give off hydrogen gas, which is explosive
option_d: Sparks can damage the charger's electronics
explanation: Vented lead-acid batteries can release hydrogen while charging. In a poorly ventilated locker, a spark from a loose connection or a dropped tool can ignite it. Lithium batteries do not give off hydrogen in normal use but have hazards of their own.

stem: What drives the alternator?
option_a: A belt from the engine's crankshaft pulley
option_b: The battery
option_c: The propeller shaft, through the gearbox
option_d: An electric motor powered from the domestic bank
explanation: The alternator is turned by a belt from the engine, so it only charges while the engine runs and the belt is in good order.

stem: The charge warning light stays on after the engine has started. What does this indicate?
option_a: The batteries are fully charged and now resting
option_b: A charging-system fault, or the alternator failing to excite
option_c: The alternator has definitely failed and needs replacing
option_d: The engine coolant is starting to overheat
explanation: The light points to a fault somewhere in the charging system, not necessarily the alternator itself. Check the belt and connections, then verify with the handbook and a voltage check; see Not charging in the Fault finder.

stem: What is the regulator's job?
option_a: Switching the starter motor on when you turn the key to start
option_b: Measuring the oil pressure and lighting the warning
option_c: Keeping the engine speed steady as the load changes
option_d: Controlling the charging voltage to avoid overcharging
explanation: Without regulation the alternator's output would rise with engine speed and could damage the batteries. The regulator holds the voltage at a safe charging level.

stem: Why should you not normally switch off the battery isolator while the engine is running?
option_a: The starter motor can engage while the engine is running
option_b: Cutting off the battery can damage the alternator's electronics
option_c: The engine will stop at once without battery power
option_d: It drains the batteries back through the alternator instead
explanation: With the battery disconnected, the alternator's output has nowhere to go and the voltage can spike, damaging its diodes or regulator. A diesel keeps running without the battery.

stem: What does the starter motor turn to start the engine?
option_a: The flywheel, through its toothed ring
option_b: The camshaft, through its drive chain
option_c: The propeller shaft, through the gearbox
option_d: The crankshaft pulley, through the belt
explanation: The starter's small gear meshes with the teeth around the flywheel, which is bolted to the crankshaft, and turns the engine over.

stem: Why is a solenoid used in the starting circuit?
option_a: So the key's small current can switch the starter's large one
option_b: To heat the air in the cylinders before starting
option_c: To store a charge of electricity, ready for the next start
option_d: To charge the battery while the engine is cranking
explanation: The starter draws far more current than a key switch could handle. The solenoid is a heavy-duty switch that the key operates with a small current.

stem: When you press the start button, nothing happens at all, not even a click. Which of these is a likely cause?
option_a: The engine oil level is below the minimum mark
option_b: The battery isolator is off or the gear lever is not in neutral
option_c: Air has been drawn into the fuel system through a loose joint
option_d: The raw water strainer is blocked with weed and debris
explanation: Complete silence usually means no current is reaching the solenoid. Fuel, cooling and oil problems do not stop the starter turning.

stem: The battery is good and its terminals are clean, but the starter turns slowly. Which connection is often overlooked?
option_a: The alternator output terminal
option_b: The fuse for the engine panel
option_c: The glow plug feed wire
option_d: The engine earth cable
explanation: Starting current returns to the battery through the engine and its earth cable. Corrosion there adds resistance and slows the starter just like a weak battery. The glow plug and alternator wiring do not carry starting current, and a blown panel fuse would stop the starter altogether.

stem: What does a glow plug do?
option_a: Warms the engine oil in the sump
option_b: Heats the combustion chamber to help a cold engine start
option_c: Creates a spark to light the fuel while the engine is running
option_d: Warms the fuel in the filter so it flows in cold weather
explanation: A diesel has no spark. The glow plug is a small heater used before and during starting so the compressed air gets hot enough to light the fuel.

stem: Why does a diesel engine find it harder to start on a cold day?
option_a: Cold air holds too little oxygen for the fuel to burn
option_b: Cold metal soaks up the compression heat, so the air may not get hot enough
option_c: The starter motor is designed to work only in warm weather
option_d: Diesel stops flowing as soon as it drops below room temperature
explanation: Compression ignition depends on the air getting very hot. A cold block and head draw heat out of the air, which is why pre-heating helps.

stem: An engine is hard to start from cold and smokes white for a minute, then runs well and restarts easily when warm. What is a likely cause?
option_a: A failed glow plug or a fault in the glow plug circuit
option_b: An alternator belt that is slipping on its drive pulley
option_c: A raw water strainer partly blocked with weed
option_d: Too much oil in the sump after an oil change
explanation: These are classic signs of poor cold starting. Once warm, the engine does not need the glow plugs, so it runs and restarts normally.

stem: Why can aerosol starting sprays be dangerous in an engine with glow plugs?
option_a: The spray stops the alternator charging the battery
option_b: The spray gets into the fuel and blocks the fine filter
option_c: The spray chills the glow plugs so they stop heating
option_d: The vapour can ignite early on the hot plugs and damage the engine
explanation: Starting spray is highly flammable. Lit by a hot glow plug or intake heater before the piston is in position, it can cause violent combustion that damages the engine. Only use it if the handbook allows.

stem: When you switch on before starting, which lights would you normally expect to come on?
option_a: The high temperature light, which stays on while running
option_b: None at all
option_c: The oil pressure light alone; the charge light comes on once the engine runs
option_d: The oil pressure and charge warning lights
explanation: With the engine stopped there is no oil pressure and no charging, so both lights come on. That shows they work. They should go out soon after starting.

stem: On a conventional negative-earth system with lead-acid batteries, which lead should you take off first when disconnecting a battery?
option_a: The negative lead
option_b: The positive lead
option_c: Either, it makes no difference
option_d: Whichever is easier to reach
explanation: On these systems the engine is connected to the negative side. With the negative removed first, a spanner touching the positive terminal and the engine cannot complete a circuit and cause a short. Other systems, such as lithium banks with a battery management system, may have their own isolation procedure.

stem: The whole engine panel is dead when you turn the key. What should you check early on?
option_a: The fuel filter, in case it is blocked with sludge
option_b: The raw water impeller, in case its vanes have broken off
option_c: The engine oil level, in case the panel has shut off
option_d: The battery isolator and the panel's fuse or circuit breaker
explanation: If nothing at all lights, power is not reaching the panel. The isolator, fuse or breaker are the simplest things that cut it off.

stem: Why should you remove metal rings and watches before working near the batteries?
option_a: Metal jewellery near the terminals slowly drains the battery's charge
option_b: A short circuit through the metal can heat it and cause severe burns
option_c: They interfere with the multimeter's voltage readings
option_d: They attract corrosion onto the battery terminals
explanation: A battery can deliver a very large current. If a ring bridges a live terminal and earth, it heats almost instantly and can burn deeply.

stem: You want to check a battery with a multimeter. Which setting and connection is safe?
option_a: The resistance setting, with the engine running
option_b: The current (amps) setting, with the probes across the battery terminals
option_c: The current setting, with one probe on the engine and one on the positive terminal
option_d: The voltage setting, with the probes across the battery terminals
explanation: A meter on its voltage setting has a high resistance, so it can be connected across the battery safely. On a current setting it is close to a short circuit: connected across a battery or to earth it can blow the meter, burn the leads and burn you.

stem: On many engines, what two things stop working if the alternator belt breaks?
option_a: Battery charging and the coolant circulating pump
option_b: The fuel lift pump and the fuel injection pump
option_c: The engine oil pump and the starter motor
option_d: The gearbox and the stern gland greaser
explanation: A single belt often drives both the alternator and the coolant pump, so a broken belt can mean no charging and rapid overheating together.

stem: What is the safe way to inspect a drive belt?
option_a: With the engine at high revs to check for slipping
option_b: With the engine at idle so you can see it moving
option_c: With the engine stopped and unable to be started
option_d: While someone else holds the start button
explanation: Belts and pulleys can trap fingers and clothing instantly. Inspect only with the engine stopped and the key removed or isolator off.

stem: You find fine black rubber dust around the pulleys. What does it usually mean?
option_a: The engine oil is old and needs changing soon
option_b: The fuel filter is shedding its paper element
option_c: Soot is leaking from the exhaust elbow into the engine space
option_d: The belt is wearing, possibly from slipping or misalignment
explanation: Rubber dust comes from the belt itself wearing away. Check the tension, the pulley alignment and the belt's condition.

stem: Why is a belt that is too tight a problem?
option_a: It stops the starter motor from turning the engine over
option_b: It makes the belt slip and squeal under load
option_c: It makes the engine burn noticeably less fuel
option_d: It overloads the bearings in the alternator and pump
explanation: Over-tightening puts a constant sideways load on the bearings of whatever the belt drives, wearing them early. Slipping and squealing come from a belt that is too slack.

stem: Why should the tension of a newly fitted belt be checked again after a short period of running?
option_a: The alternator creeps further away from the engine as it wears
option_b: New belts shrink as they warm up and become too tight
option_c: New belts bed in and stretch slightly, so they can become slack
option_d: The first run can flip the belt over so it sits the wrong way round
explanation: A new belt settles into its pulleys and stretches a little at first. Rechecking catches the extra slack before it starts to slip.

stem: What lets the engine run while the propeller is not turning?
option_a: Switching off the alternator
option_b: Loosening the stern gland
option_c: Closing the raw water seacock fully
option_d: Putting the gearbox in neutral
explanation: In neutral the gearbox disconnects the engine from the shaft, so the engine can warm up or charge the batteries without driving the boat.

stem: What is the right way to change from ahead to astern?
option_a: Stop the engine, select astern, then restart the engine
option_b: Go straight from ahead to astern without changing the revs
option_c: Bring the engine to idle, pause briefly in neutral, then select astern
option_d: Raise the revs in neutral, then select astern quickly
explanation: Changing at idle with a short pause lets the shaft slow before the gearbox engages the other direction, avoiding shock loads on the gearbox and coupling. Follow your gearbox handbook if it says otherwise.

stem: Where should you check the gearbox oil level on most installations?
option_a: On the engine oil dipstick, because they share oil
option_b: In the fuel filter bowl
option_c: On the gearbox's own dipstick or level plug
option_d: In the coolant header tank
explanation: Most gearboxes have their own separate oil supply with its own dipstick or level plug, and may need a different type of oil from the engine.

stem: With the engine warm and the lever in neutral, the boat drives steadily forward as if in gear. What is a likely cause?
option_a: The propeller is fouled with weed
option_b: The gear cable is out of adjustment
option_c: The cutless bearing is worn and lets the shaft drag
option_d: The engine's idle speed is set slightly too high
explanation: If the cable has stretched or slipped, the lever and gearbox positions no longer match, and the gearbox may stay partly engaged. Some gearboxes drag slightly in neutral when cold, which can be normal, but steady drive in neutral is not. Idle speed, bearing wear and fouling do not make a gearbox drive in neutral.

stem: Apart from ahead, neutral and astern, what else does a marine gearbox usually do?
option_a: Cools the engine oil before it returns to the engine sump
option_b: Pumps raw cooling water through to the engine
option_c: Reduces the shaft speed compared with the engine speed
option_d: Charges the batteries through a second alternator
explanation: Propellers work best turning slower than a diesel engine, so most gearboxes include a reduction ratio.

stem: What is the job of the stern gland?
option_a: To keep water out where the shaft passes through the hull
option_b: To hold the propeller firmly on the tapered end of the shaft
option_c: To cool the gearbox oil using the water outside
option_d: To connect the shaft to the gearbox output flange
explanation: The shaft has to pass through the hull to reach the propeller. The stern gland seals around it while still letting it turn.

stem: A traditional packed stern gland drips slowly while the shaft turns. What does this usually mean?
option_a: The packing has failed and the gland needs repacking now
option_b: It may be normal: many packed glands use water to cool and lubricate
option_c: The cutless bearing has worn and needs replacing
option_d: The gland should be tightened straight away until all dripping stops
explanation: Many packed glands are meant to drip slightly in use; how much is normal depends on the gland and its maker. Tightening until all dripping stops can overheat the packing and wear the shaft. A new or increasing leak is different: treat it as urgent.

stem: What can happen if a packed stern gland is tightened too much?
option_a: The packing overheats and wears a groove in the shaft
option_b: The gland stops dripping and the shaft runs cooler
option_c: The propeller works loose and eventually falls off the shaft
option_d: The gearbox can no longer be put into gear
explanation: Too much pressure stops the water reaching the packing. Friction then heats it and wears the shaft, which can be costly to repair. A dry gland is not a sign that all is well.

stem: A shaft seal that its maker says should not drip shows a steady trickle of water. How should you treat it?
option_a: As normal, because every kind of shaft seal drips a little
option_b: As something to look at when the boat is next lifted out
option_c: As a sign that the seal needs more grease pumping in
option_d: As an urgent fault, checking the bilge pumps can keep up
explanation: A seal designed not to drip should stay dry. A leak can mean wear, damage or a problem with its hose, and it is below the waterline, so new or increasing leakage is a vessel-safety issue: leaving it until the boat is next lifted out risks flooding. Check the bilge, make sure the pumps can keep up and get the seal looked at.

stem: When is it safe to adjust the stern gland?
option_a: Only with the engine stopped and unable to be started
option_b: Only with the engine running in astern at idle
option_c: At any time, because the shaft is safely behind a guard
option_d: Only while the shaft is turning slowly in gear
explanation: A turning shaft can catch clothing, fingers or tools. Make sure it cannot turn before working near it.

stem: After a passage the bilge is filling faster than usual, and water is coming from the shaft seal. What should you do first?
option_a: Pump the bilge dry and carry on unless the leak gets worse
option_b: Stop the shaft once safe, check the pumps keep up, and get help if it gains
option_c: Tighten the seal with the shaft turning so you can see the leak slow down
option_d: Keep motoring to harbour and look at the seal when next lifted out
explanation: An uncontrolled leak at the shaft seal is a vessel-safety issue. Stop the shaft once it is safe, make sure pumping keeps up, and call for assistance early if the water is gaining. Never adjust a seal on a turning shaft.

stem: A rope has wrapped round the propeller. What must you do before trying to clear it?
option_a: Stop the engine and make sure it cannot be started
option_b: Leave the engine in neutral while you clear it
option_c: Run the engine at full power ahead to cut through it
option_d: Put the engine in astern to unwind it
explanation: Even in neutral, a gearbox can drag or be knocked into gear. Stopping and isolating the engine is the only safe state for working near the propeller.

stem: What lubricates a typical cutless bearing?
option_a: The water the boat is floating in
option_b: Grease from the stern gland greaser
option_c: Engine oil pumped from the sump
option_d: Gearbox oil
explanation: The cutless bearing has a grooved rubber lining that lets water flow through, lubricating and cooling it.

stem: With the boat out of the water, the shaft can be moved sideways in the bearing where it leaves the hull. What does this suggest?
option_a: The cutless bearing may be worn
option_b: The gearbox oil is low
option_c: The shaft anode has worn away
option_d: The stern gland packing needs adjusting
explanation: A good bearing supports the shaft closely, so noticeable sideways movement is a clue that the rubber lining has worn. Check it against the bearing maker's tolerances, or ask an engineer.

stem: Why can a fouled propeller make the engine produce black smoke?
option_a: The fouling blocks the exhaust outlet under the water
option_b: Weed is drawn into the engine's air filter and clogs it
option_c: Barnacles on the propeller release oil that is drawn into the exhaust
option_d: The extra load calls for more fuel than the air can burn cleanly
explanation: Extra drag means more load. The engine is supplied with more fuel to keep its speed, but there is not enough air to burn it all, which shows as black smoke.

stem: Over a season, vibration under power slowly gets worse and the stern gland starts to leak more. What should you suspect?
option_a: A weak engine battery that is losing its charge
option_b: Too much oil left in the engine after the last oil change
option_c: A fuel filter that is slowly blocking with sludge
option_d: Worn engine mounts or poor alignment between engine and shaft
explanation: If the engine sags on worn mounts or is out of line with the shaft, the shaft runs off-centre, causing vibration and wearing the gland and cutless bearing.

stem: Why is it useful to look in the bilge under the engine before starting?
option_a: To check the battery charge by looking at its indicator
option_b: Fresh oil, fuel or coolant there points to a leak and where to look
option_c: To check the fuel level through the fuel tank's inspection hatch
option_d: To check that the propeller is clear of weed and rope
explanation: Fluids that leak from the engine collect in the bilge beneath it. Spotting them before starting lets you trace a leak while it is still minor.

stem: What should you check immediately after the engine starts?
option_a: That the stern gland is dripping fast enough to cool it
option_b: That the fuel gauge shows the tank is completely full
option_c: That the warning lights are out and water is coming from the exhaust
option_d: That the batteries have been switched off to save charge
explanation: These two checks confirm that the oil pressure, charging and raw water cooling are all working before you rely on the engine.

stem: Why is it worth doing your pre-start checks in the same order every time?
option_a: It makes the engine warm up faster
option_b: A fixed routine makes it much harder to miss a check
option_c: The checks must be done in the order printed on the panel
option_d: The engine will not start if the order changes
explanation: Routine turns the checks into a habit, so a missing step feels wrong. Changing the order each time makes it easy to skip something.

stem: Why should you let the engine warm gently before using full power?
option_a: The gearbox will not engage properly until its oil is warm
option_b: Cold diesel is too thick for the injection pump at high revs
option_c: Oil flows and protects best once warm, and parts expand evenly
option_d: The alternator needs time to recharge the battery before taking load
explanation: Cold oil is thick and reaches bearings more slowly, and a cold engine has tighter clearances in some places. A gentle warm-up reduces wear.

stem: Before starting, you see a thin film of oil and a little coolant in the bilge that was not there yesterday. What should you do?
option_a: Find the source before relying on the engine, starting with levels and hoses
option_b: Pump the bilge out over the side and carry on as planned
option_c: Start the engine and run it hard for a while to see whether the leak gets worse
option_d: Top up the oil and coolant, then ignore it unless it gets worse
explanation: New fluid in the bilge means something has changed. Checking levels and tracing the leak first can prevent an engine failure later. Running the engine hard to see whether a leak gets worse can turn a small fault into a failure or a fire, and oily water must not be pumped overboard.

stem: You have started the engine and are about to engage gear for the first time. Where it is safe and practicable, what should you check first?
option_a: That the stern gland is dripping steadily
option_b: That the fuel tank is more than half full
option_c: That the propeller is clear of lines and people
option_d: That the engine has reached full working temperature
explanation: A line or fender caught round the propeller can stall the engine and damage the shaft, and anyone in the water near it is in danger. Look before you engage gear.

stem: Where should you find the service schedule for your engine?
option_a: On the engine's identification plate
option_b: On the battery label
option_c: In the engine manufacturer's handbook
option_d: In the boat's insurance policy documents
explanation: The handbook lists each service job and when it is due. Intervals vary between engines, so the handbook is the reference.

stem: A service is due 'by running hours or by time, whichever comes first'. Your engine has done few hours this year. What does this mean?
option_a: The service is due only once both limits have been reached
option_b: The service is still due once the time limit is reached
option_c: The service is no longer needed
option_d: The service can wait until the running hours are reached
explanation: Oil ages, rubber parts perish and corrosion continues even when the engine is not used. That is why there is a time limit as well as an hours limit.

stem: Why is it useful to keep a written log of engine maintenance?
option_a: It replaces the need to keep the engine handbook on board
option_b: It is required by law for every leisure boat with an inboard engine
option_c: It makes the engine use noticeably less fuel each season
option_d: It shows what is due next and helps an engineer track down faults
explanation: A log of dates, hours and parts tells you when jobs are due and gives an engineer a history to work from. It also adds value when you sell the boat.

stem: Which of these jobs is normally one for a qualified engineer rather than the owner?
option_a: Changing the engine oil
option_b: Servicing the injectors
option_c: Cleaning the raw water strainer
option_d: Draining water from the fuel filter bowl
explanation: Injectors need specialist equipment to test and set them. The other jobs are routine owner maintenance.

stem: Where one is fitted, what shows how many running hours the engine has done?
option_a: The engine hour meter
option_b: The tachometer (rev counter)
option_c: The service sticker on the oil filter
option_d: The temperature gauge
explanation: The hour meter records how long the engine has run, and many service intervals are based on it. Not every engine has one; without it, keep a written log of running time.

stem: Why is the engine oil usually changed before the winter lay-up rather than in spring?
option_a: So the engine is not left standing all winter in acidic used oil
option_b: So the engine turns over faster on the first spring start
option_c: Because new oil can freeze in the bottle if it is left until spring
option_d: So the oil has the winter to settle before the first start
explanation: Used oil contains acids from combustion. Leaving it in the engine for months encourages corrosion, so fresh oil goes in before lay-up.

stem: What is the main risk of leaving sea water in the raw water circuit in a hard frost?
option_a: It makes the engine oil too thick to pump in spring
option_b: It slowly drains the batteries through the engine
option_c: It can freeze and crack the pump, heat exchanger or other parts
option_d: It breeds diesel bug, which then spreads into the fuel
explanation: Water expands when it freezes, and the force can split castings and pipes. Handbooks explain whether to drain the circuit or fill it with antifreeze.

stem: You block the exhaust outlet and air intake for the winter. What else should you do?
option_a: Note it in a logbook that you keep at home
option_b: Paint over them so they stay watertight
option_c: Put a clear note on the engine controls to remove them before starting
option_d: Nothing, because the engine will push the blanks out as soon as it starts
explanation: Starting with the intake or exhaust blocked can cause serious damage. A note on the controls makes sure whoever starts the engine next removes them.

stem: When recommissioning, why should you check the stern seal and through-hull fittings once the boat is afloat?
option_a: Hose clips loosen over winter and are easiest to tighten afloat
option_b: Out of the water nothing is pressing on them, so leaks cannot show
option_c: Through-hull fittings are checked by the insurer at each launch
option_d: Antifreeze left in them over winter has to be flushed out first
explanation: Out of the water there is nothing to leak. Checking straight after launch catches a perished hose, a loose clip or a seal that needs attention before you leave.

stem: Why should batteries be kept charged over the winter?
option_a: Charging keeps the alternator bearings from seizing
option_b: A flat battery left in the cold can be permanently damaged
option_c: Charged batteries give off a little heat that keeps the engine warm
option_d: Charging keeps the stern gland's seal from drying out
explanation: Many batteries are damaged if left discharged, and a flat battery is more likely to be harmed by frost. A suitable charger or regular charging prevents this.

stem: Which of these is an essential engine spare to carry on board?
option_a: A complete spare cylinder head assembly and gasket
option_b: A spare crankshaft and set of bearings
option_c: A raw water impeller with its cover gasket
option_d: A complete second gearbox, ready to fit
explanation: Impellers wear out and fail without warning, and changing one is a common at-sea repair. Major engine parts are not practical spares.

stem: Why should you carry spare fuel filter elements?
option_a: Fuel filters need changing every time you go out
option_b: Blocked fuel filters are a common reason for an engine stopping
option_c: Spare elements are needed to bleed the fuel system
option_d: The engine will not start once a filter is a year old
explanation: Rough weather can stir up dirt that blocks a filter quickly. A spare element and the tools to fit it can get the engine running again at sea.

stem: What is the point of checking that your spare belt and tools fit while you are in harbour?
option_a: Because spares slowly wear out if they are never used
option_b: So you know the repair is possible before you need to do it at sea
option_c: So the spares stay warm and supple until they are needed
option_d: Because the boat's warranty needs the spares to be tried
explanation: A belt of the wrong size or a spanner that does not fit is only discovered when you try to use it. Trying in calm conditions avoids nasty surprises.

stem: Which of these is most useful for a temporary repair to a leaking cooling hose?
option_a: Ordinary duct tape
option_b: Electrical insulating tape
option_c: Bathroom silicone sealant
option_d: Self-amalgamating tape
explanation: Self-amalgamating tape fuses to itself when stretched and wrapped, making a tight seal that can hold until the hose is replaced. Ordinary tapes and sealants do not hold against water pressure and heat.

stem: Why is it worth recording part numbers for your filters, impeller and belt in your log?
option_a: Once recorded, any make of filter can be used safely
option_b: Recording them is a legal requirement for all leisure boats
option_c: The insurer needs them before it will cover the engine
option_d: So you can order the right parts quickly and avoid ones that do not fit
explanation: Similar-looking parts often differ in size, thread or rating. Having the exact numbers to hand means you get the right part first time, even from a chandler far from home.

stem: In the WOBBLE memory aid for engine checks, what do the letters stand for?
option_a: Water, Oil, Belts, Bilges, Leaks and levels, Exhaust
option_b: Water, Oil, Batteries, Bearings, Lights, Engine
option_c: Water, Oil, Bolts, Bilges, Lights, Electrics
option_d: Wiring, Oil, Belts, Batteries, Lubrication, Exhaust
explanation: WOBBLE covers the coolant and raw water, oil, drive belts, bilges, leaks and fuel and battery levels, and finally the exhaust once the engine is running.

stem: Which WOBBLE check is made with the engine running rather than before it starts?
option_a: Belts: wear, cracking and tension
option_b: Oil: the level on the dipstick
option_c: Bilges: no water, oil or fuel under the engine
option_d: Exhaust: cooling water coming out of the exhaust
explanation: The E is the only check that needs the engine running: water from a wet exhaust shows the raw water pump is delivering. Belts, bilges and oil are checked with the engine off.

stem: You start the engine and after several seconds no cooling water is coming out of the wet exhaust. What should you do?
option_a: Carry on, as the water will appear once the engine is warm
option_b: Stop the engine and find the cause before running it again
option_c: Raise the revs to help the pump draw water through
option_d: Leave it at tickover and check again in ten minutes
explanation: With no water flow the engine and the wet exhaust are not being cooled, and the impeller is running dry. Raising the revs or leaving it running can damage the impeller, exhaust hose and silencer within a short time and overheat the engine.

stem: During your pre-start checks the engine oil on the dipstick looks milky. What should you do?
option_a: Start the engine and run it hard to drive off the moisture
option_b: Leave the engine off and get advice from a qualified engineer
option_c: Top it up with fresh oil and start as normal
option_d: Change the oil filter and carry on with the trip
explanation: Milky oil suggests water or coolant is mixing with it. Running the engine on contaminated oil can damage the bearings, and topping up or changing the filter hides the problem without finding where the water is coming from.

stem: Shortly after starting, you realise the raw-water seacock was left closed. What should you do?
option_a: Increase the revs so the pump can draw water past the closed seacock
option_b: Stop the engine, open the seacock, and check the impeller and water flow before relying on the engine
option_c: Leave it closed until the engine has warmed up, then open it
option_d: Open the seacock with the engine running and carry on without further checks
explanation: Running with the seacock closed lets the impeller run dry, which can damage its vanes within a short time, and leaves the wet exhaust uncooled. Carrying on without checking risks an overheated engine or a burnt exhaust hose later in the trip.

stem: Why should the freshwater coolant level be checked only with the engine cold?
option_a: A hot pressure cap can release scalding coolant when opened
option_b: The header tank empties itself while the engine is warm
option_c: The thermostat sticks open if the cap is removed when warm
option_d: Antifreeze loses its strength if it meets air while hot
explanation: A warm cooling system is under pressure. Opening the cap lets the coolant boil and spray out, which can scald you. Wait until the engine is cold.
