stem: With the engine running and warm, you want to look again for leaks. How should you do it?
option_a: Feel along the hoses near the belts by hand to find damp patches
option_b: Look carefully, keeping hands, clothing and hair well clear of belts, pulleys and the shaft
option_c: Take off the belt guard so you can see behind the pulleys
option_d: Hold a rag against the drive belt to see whether it picks up oil
explanation: With the engine running, a hand, sleeve or rag near a belt, pulley or shaft can be caught and pulled in, causing serious injury. Check by eye only; touch nothing near moving parts until the engine is stopped.

stem: What should you check about the drive belts before starting?
option_a: That they are as tight as you can possibly make them
option_b: That they show no wear, cracking or fraying, and are tensioned as the handbook specifies
option_c: That they have been dressed with oil so they do not squeal
option_d: That they are slack enough to lift off the pulleys by hand
explanation: A worn or wrongly tensioned belt can slip or break, stopping the raw water pump or alternator. Too tight a belt loads the bearings, and oil on a belt makes it slip; follow the handbook's tension.

stem: Before starting the engine, where should the gear lever be?
option_a: In astern, to hold the boat back against its lines
option_b: Anywhere, because the gearbox always disengages for starting
option_c: In ahead, so the boat moves off as soon as it starts
option_d: In neutral
explanation: Starting in gear can make the boat lurch into a pontoon, another boat or a person in the water, and can strain the lines. Some installations will not crank unless the lever is in neutral, but do not rely on that; check it every time.

stem: Your engine stops while you are motoring near a rocky shore. What should you do first?
option_a: Open the engine space and start looking for the fault
option_b: Keep trying to start the engine until it runs
option_c: Make the boat safe: sail, anchor or call for help
option_d: Check the fuel filter bowl for water straight away
explanation: The boat's safety comes before the engine. Opening up the engine or cranking it while the boat drifts towards rocks puts everyone in danger. Once you are no longer at risk, you can work on the engine calmly.

stem: Why is it useful to ask 'what changed recently?' when an engine develops a fault?
option_a: It tells you which part to replace without any further checks
option_b: Recent events, such as refuelling, often point straight to the cause
option_c: It is the first question an insurer will ask after a claim
option_d: It tells you how old the engine is and when it was built
explanation: A fault that appears after refuelling suggests fuel quality; after a filter change, air or a poor seal. Linking the fault to a recent event narrows the search quickly.

stem: Which three things does a diesel engine need in order to run?
option_a: A gearbox, a propeller and a stern gland
option_b: Clean fuel free of air, clean air, and good compression
option_c: A charged battery, clean fuel and cooling water
option_d: Coolant, a fully charged battery and a full fuel tank
explanation: Compression heats the air, the fuel is injected and burns. If any of the three is missing, the engine will not run. Cooling, lubrication and electrics matter too, but for keeping going and starting.

stem: Why should you change only one thing at a time when fault finding?
option_a: So the engine does not need bleeding more than once
option_b: So you can tell which change fixed the problem, without adding new faults
option_c: So the job takes longer and is therefore done more carefully
option_d: Because most engine tools are designed to be used one at a time
explanation: If you change several things and the engine runs, you will not know which mattered. Each extra change also adds a chance of a new problem, such as letting air into the fuel.

stem: In what order should you usually check possible causes?
option_a: Whichever parts of the engine are easiest to reach
option_b: Simple and common causes first, difficult and rare ones later
option_c: Internal engine parts first, then the outside ones
option_d: The most expensive parts first, as they matter most
explanation: Most faults have simple causes such as a control left in the wrong place, a blocked filter or a closed valve. Checking those first saves time and avoids unnecessary dismantling.

stem: Your engine stops while you are crossing a busy channel. Which order of actions is best?
option_a: Make the boat safe, then change both fuel filters straight away
option_b: Check the simple causes first, gather the clues, then make the boat safe
option_c: Make the boat safe, gather the clues, then check the simple causes first
option_d: Gather the clues, try restarting several times, then make the boat safe
explanation: The boat comes first: trying to restart while drifting in a busy channel puts the boat at risk of collision. Once it is safe, note how the engine stopped and what changed, then check the easy causes before dismantling anything or changing parts on a guess.

stem: The engine turns over at normal speed but will not fire. Which is a sensible first check?
option_a: The battery terminals, because a weak battery causes this
option_b: The raw water strainer, because a blocked one stops it firing
option_c: That the stop control is fully home, then the fuel supply
option_d: The starter solenoid, because it may not be engaging fully
explanation: If the engine turns normally, the battery and starter are doing their job. Sensible first checks are the stop control and then the fuel; on a cold day, pre-heating; on an electronic engine, any fault warning or inhibit. A blocked air intake or low compression are further possibilities.

stem: Pressing start gives a single click and nothing else. What does this usually point to?
option_a: A fuel shut-off valve that was left closed at the tank
option_b: A raw water strainer blocked with weed
option_c: Air in the fuel lines to the injection pump
option_d: A weak battery or a poor connection to the starter
explanation: The click is the solenoid trying to engage. Without enough current, the starter cannot turn. Fuel and cooling faults do not stop the engine turning over.

stem: The engine will not start on a cold morning but starts easily later in the day. Which part is a likely suspect?
option_a: The glow plugs or their circuit
option_b: The stern gland and its packing rings
option_c: The level of the gearbox oil
option_d: The raw water pump impeller
explanation: Cold starting relies on extra heat from the glow plugs. Once the air is warmer the engine manages without them, which hides the fault.

stem: Why can long periods of cranking be harmful on an engine with a wet exhaust?
option_a: Unburnt diesel floods the cylinders and washes the oil off the bores
option_b: The raw water pump runs dry while the engine is only cranking
option_c: The exhaust gets dangerously hot while the engine is cranking
option_d: Water pumped into the exhaust is not blown out and can flood the cylinders
explanation: While cranking, the raw water pump still pushes water into the exhaust, but there is no exhaust gas flow to expel it, so water can build up and reach the cylinders. If repeated cranking fails, stop and follow the engine and exhaust maker's procedure; never run the engine with the seacock closed.

stem: While cranking, the engine turns a little and then stops hard. What should you do?
option_a: Keep cranking, using a freshly charged battery to give more power
option_b: Bleed the fuel system, then try cranking again straight away
option_c: Stop cranking and get advice, because water may be in the cylinders
option_d: Use a starting spray to help it fire before it stops
explanation: Water does not compress. If a cylinder is full of it, forcing the engine round, with more cranking or a starting spray, can bend a connecting rod. Do not crank again; get qualified assistance.

stem: After several attempts, an engine with a wet exhaust still will not start. What should you do?
option_a: Keep cranking in longer bursts so the exhaust can clear itself
option_b: Close the seacock and keep cranking until it fires, then open it
option_c: Stop cranking and follow the engine and exhaust maker's procedure
option_d: Use a starting spray so it fires before the exhaust fills
explanation: Repeated cranking can let water build up in a wet exhaust and enter the engine. Follow the documented procedure for your installation, and never run the engine with the raw-water seacock closed: an engine that fires with it shut quickly destroys its impeller and exhaust. Longer cranking or a starting spray only adds to the risk, and if water may have got in, do not crank again.

stem: The engine slows and fades over several seconds before stopping. What type of cause does this usually point to?
option_a: A rope round the propeller
option_b: Low oil pressure
option_c: A fuel supply problem
option_d: A failed glow plug
explanation: A gradual fade is typical of fuel starvation, such as a blocked filter or air in the fuel, as the supply dwindles. A rope usually stops the engine abruptly, a glow plug affects only starting, and low oil pressure would set off its alarm.

stem: The engine runs fine in neutral but stalls as soon as you put it in gear. What is the best response?
option_a: Assume the gearbox has failed and call for a tow without checking anything
option_b: Raise the idle speed with the throttle and keep engaging gear until it holds
option_c: Engage astern at higher revs to unwind whatever may be caught
option_d: Stop the engine, make sure it cannot start, then check for something round the propeller
explanation: Something round the propeller is one important possibility, but a low idle speed, a gearbox fault or a binding shaft can do the same. Make the engine safe before inspecting near the propeller, and rule things out one at a time. Forcing it in gear or at higher revs can wrap a rope tighter and damage the shaft, gearbox or stern gear.

stem: Over a season, the boat gets slower at the same engine revs and the exhaust smokes black under load. What is a likely cause?
option_a: A fouled hull or propeller adding load
option_b: A slipping alternator belt robbing power
option_c: A worn cutless bearing letting the shaft vibrate
option_d: Water in the fuel, which burns poorly
explanation: Growth on the hull and propeller adds drag. The engine works harder, burns more fuel than it can use cleanly, and the boat goes slower.

stem: The engine stops, restarts after a rest, runs for a while and stops again, with no water or dirt in the filter bowl. What might be blocked?
option_a: The oil filter
option_b: The fuel tank vent
option_c: The exhaust water injection
option_d: The raw water strainer
explanation: With a blocked vent, a vacuum builds in the tank as fuel is used until the lift pump cannot draw any more. Resting lets air leak back in slowly, so the cycle repeats.

stem: After a rough passage the engine fades over a few seconds and stops. Where should you look first?
option_a: In the coolant header tank, to check the coolant level
option_b: In the primary fuel filter bowl, for water and dirt
option_c: At the alternator belt, for its tension and wear
option_d: At the stern gland, for a faster drip than usual
explanation: A fading stop points to fuel starvation, and rough water stirs up water and sediment from the bottom of the tank. The primary filter bowl shows quickly whether any has come through.

stem: Which two warnings mean you should stop the engine as soon as it is safe to do so?
option_a: Low oil pressure and high temperature
option_b: High temperature and the charge warning
option_c: The charge warning and low fuel
option_d: Low oil pressure and the glow plug light
explanation: Both are stop-engine conditions: reduce power and stop as soon as the boat is safe, and do not restart until the cause is found and corrected. A charge warning needs prompt attention, mainly because the belt may also drive the coolant pump.

stem: The engine overheated although water was flowing normally from the exhaust. Once it has stopped and cooled, which of these should you check?
option_a: The drive belt and the coolant level
option_b: The raw water seacock
option_c: The raw water strainer
option_d: Whether the raw water pump has an impeller fitted
explanation: Normal exhaust water shows the raw water side is working. The problem is more likely on the coolant side: a slipping belt, low coolant, the thermostat or a blocked heat exchanger.

stem: What does blue exhaust smoke usually mean?
option_a: There is unburnt fuel from a cold start
option_b: The exhaust is short of cooling water
option_c: The engine is burning lubricating oil
option_d: The engine has too much fuel for its air
explanation: Oil burning in the cylinders gives a bluish smoke. Black smoke points to excess fuel, white smoke on a cold start to unburnt fuel, and steam to a cooling problem.

stem: The charge warning light comes on while motoring. Why should you check the drive belt straight away?
option_a: If the belt also drives the coolant pump, the engine will soon overheat
option_b: Because the belt helps keep the propeller shaft in line
option_c: Because a broken belt will quickly cause low oil pressure
option_d: Because on most engines the same belt drives the fuel injection pump
explanation: A charge warning indicates a charging-system fault, and on many engines the alternator belt also drives the coolant circulating pump. The warning can therefore be the first sign of an overheating problem to come.

stem: You suspect a temperature alarm is false because the engine does not feel hot. What is the safe approach?
option_a: Treat the alarm as real until you have proved otherwise
option_b: Remove the pressure cap to check the coolant
option_c: Disconnect the alarm and carry on
option_d: Increase revs to see if it clears
explanation: Sensors can fail, but so can engines. Ignoring a real warning risks expensive damage, and opening a hot pressure cap risks scalding. Stop, check safely, and get advice if unsure.
